newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD -U.S., Britain vie for market attention.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD -U.S., Britain vie for market attention.

text.p: Prospects of an interest rate rise in Britain will vie for investors' attention in the coming week with the performance of the U.S. bond market, analysts said.
The effect of the larger-than-expected rise in U.S. non-farm payrolls, which sparked a fall of a point and a half in the long bond on Friday, was expected to ripple out into the coming week.

"The most important thing is what has happened today and how things pan out after that," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase in London. "The moves in the international asset markets are going to be key for all markets," he said.

In Britain investors are watching for a rise in base rates, currently 6.0 percent, but weaker-than-expected manufacturing data released on Friday may have decreased the likelihood of a rate hike next week.
On Wednesday, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George hold their monthly meeting.

"I think George will lobby hard for a rise, but Clarke will rebuff him, using the strength of sterling, weak manufacturing data and disappointing Christmas sales to back himself up," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
A Reuters poll of analysts showed a slim majority expect rates to remain unchanged after the meeting. March short sterling futures are discounting a 50 basis point rise.
"There is enormous political pressure on Clarke not to raise rates at all, and he will try very hard to avoid it," said Stamenkovic.

But Robert Prior, international economist at HSBC James Capel, said he expected the chancellor to raise rates by 25 basis points to get the move out of the way as soon as possible and well before the general election due by late May.

British December retail prices, due for release on Thursday, were forecast to show a monthly rise of 0.4 percent and a year-on-year rise of 2.5 percent. The underlying figure was forecast at 3.1 percent.
Stamenkovic said the figures would support the picture of benign inflation and back up leaving interest rates alone.
There were few economic releases of note elsewhere in Europe, analysts said.
In the U.S., December retail sales and consumer price data for December were due on Tuesday. Industrial production and capacity utilisation were scheduled for Friday.
Stamenkovic said the data were likely to be bond-friendly, but would not be soft enough to change underlying sentiment.
"These are not going to be conclusive figures as far as the market is concerned," he said.

Prior said retail sales and production data would need to be significantly robust to put a rate hike on the agenda at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting. The committee next meets to discuss interest rate policy on February 4.

"While the economy is showing signs of strength in the first quarter as lower long term interest rates feed through, it won't be enough to provoke the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates," said Prior.
Prior expected retail sales to rise 0.2 percent, and industrial production to rise 0.3 percent.

In Japan, the major concern is the performance of the equity market. Analysts said persistent losses in the stock market, although currently supporting bonds, would start to trigger selling in the bond markets if they continued.
